# Lucas Dantas

> Backend Engineer based in São Gonçalo, RJ, Brazil. Open to senior backend roles · remote · UTC−3.

At Personare I moved ~15 payment and cart APIs off a PHP monolith to Go on AWS Lambda. Infrastructure costs dropped about 30% and read routes went from ~3s to ~5 ms. Checkout now handles ~10M requests and ~11k paid orders a month.

Backend engineer since 2017, freelancing since 2015. Go and serverless on AWS are home. I also write TypeScript and React when the product needs it, which is how I ship my side projects end to end. I got into this because building things is fun, and it still is.

I like ambiguous briefs and owning them end to end. On Longa, for example, I picked a rules engine over ML: less magic, but every plan change can explain itself, and it runs on the device with zero inference cost.

The site is available in English (https://lucantas.github.io/portfolio/) and Brazilian Portuguese (https://lucantas.github.io/portfolio/pt/).

## Experience

### Software Engineer · Personare (Jun 2022 – present)

- Acted as backend lead on an engineering team of up to 10, reporting directly to the CTO. Bootstrapped the Go backend monorepo and its conventions (spec-first workflow, dependency boundaries, 80% coverage gates, OpenAPI contract tests), which the team adopted as its standard.
- Ran the spike, wrote the stories and led the migration of ~15 payment and cart APIs from a PHP monolith to Go on AWS Lambda in 8 weeks, redesigning a rigid API contract with no rollback needed. Checkout now serves ~10M requests and ~11k paid orders a month across card, Pix, PayPal, Apple Pay and Google Pay.
- Moved post-purchase work (confirmation email, analytics, Salesforce sync) off the critical path onto EventBridge and SQS with DLQs on the queue-backed steps, so a downstream failure never blocks a purchase. Added idempotency to retried flows and a transactional outbox.
- Designed and shipped invoice issuing on Brazil's national e-invoice system (NFS-e) ahead of its 2026 legal deadline: ~11k invoices a month, 115k+ so far, 0.03% left pending.
- Root-caused a 27% drop in an email alert product sending ~2.2M emails a day within 3 hours of detection, recalculated 1.25M users and wrote the postmortem.
- Introduced alarms as code across 12+ services, where detection used to depend on users complaining, then removed ~107 noisy alarms so the rest get acted on.
- Hardened payment security: a legacy card vault stopped retaining PAN and CVV, fixed open-redirect and authorization flaws, and led the same-day patch of a critical PHP-FPM RCE.
- Moved a legacy WordPress commerce service from a single EC2 host to ECS Fargate and Aurora Serverless v2 with Terraform, runbooks and a rehearsed rollback.
- Initiated and co-led the new internal admin (Next.js, plus Go on 15 Lambdas with an audit trail) that gives Support, Marketing and Product self-service.
- On the Go astrology APIs (100M+ invocations a month), built the eclipses endpoint and migrated the Professional Chart from PHP with tests that diff it against the legacy output.

Stack: Go · Node.js · TypeScript · Next.js · React · AWS Lambda/SAM · AppSync GraphQL · CloudWatch · Terraform · MySQL · PostgreSQL · DynamoDB · Docker

## Project details

### Longa: Training plans that adapt to how you actually ran

Most training plans are static. Skip runs and the schedule ignores it. Longa builds a plan from a short assessment and, when you log an incomplete long run, a lost week or an injury, rewrites the weeks ahead with less volume and hard sessions turned easy. It never touches the current week or the race date.

I built it solo, end to end: an Expo/React Native app that runs on web and Android, a Go API on Fly.io with Postgres, and a dependency-free TypeScript plan engine that runs on the device. Every change explains itself in plain language, so the runner knows why the week looks different.

It also records runs by GPS with a map, imports from Health Connect, syncs local-first with last-write-wins and bills through Stripe, in three languages. It's live on the web and still pre-launch: Android passes the end-to-end suite but isn't in the store yet.

### Morada: Condominium management for admins and residents

I built it for a real small building. The admin registers apartments and residents, issues the monthly fee, records expenses with their proofs and sends notices. Residents see their receipts, pay via Pix, upload the proof and follow the building's balance.

The ledger is keyed by apartment rather than by person, so a resident can move out and the unit keeps its whole history. It's TypeScript end to end: React 19 on Cloudflare Pages, a Hono API on Fly.io, Postgres on Neon and proofs on R2. Everything scales to zero, so it costs about nothing to run.

I built it feature-first, with lint enforcing the boundaries in both apps, and test-first the whole way: 900+ tests behind an 80% coverage gate, Playwright end to end in CI, and a check that ties every commit to a written spec. When main goes green it deploys itself.

### Diário SG: São Gonçalo's official gazettes, made searchable

São Gonçalo publishes two official gazettes, one from City Hall and one from the City Council, as long PDFs that hardly anyone reads. I built a pipeline that downloads each edition, runs OCR on scanned pages, splits it into acts like appointments, contracts, tenders and decrees, and indexes them for Portuguese full-text search. The index holds 5,286 editions since 2010, about 162,000 acts. A second collector pulls nearly 50,000 City Council bills from 2014 on, works out each one's stage from its procedural history and links a bill to the law it became, so you can see which ones have sat in committee for months.

You can search by name, CNPJ or subject and filter by act type, gazette, agency and theme, like the environment. A company's page puts the acts that cite it next to its federal tax registry record, CGU sanctions, TCE-RJ payments, City Hall spending commitments and PNCP contracts. Dashboards rank the largest suppliers and flag patterns worth a second look, like a no-bid purchase split into smaller ones or a newly opened company that gets an environmental licence. Save a term, CNPJ or process number, or just a set of filters, and you get an email when a new edition mentions it, or follow any search over RSS.

There's also an MCP server. Each person generates a key and plugs the gazette into Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor, with 12 tools to search, read and cross-check acts. It's written in Go with clean architecture and events between the scraper and the worker, and Postgres handles search with unaccent and trigram indexes. Caching the OCR output took reindexing a month from almost 10 minutes to 5 seconds. It runs live at diariosg.com.br on free tiers: collection and data loads on scheduled GitHub Actions, the API and site on Render, Postgres on Neon. To fit the 1 GB database limit I swapped a 224 MB trigram index for a 20 MB one over the numbers in each act, with the same search results. Terraform keeps a Google Cloud version ready.
